extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and research-integrity professionals interested in publication ethics and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and red flags editors and publishers use to detect problematic submissions (AI-generated text, citation manipulation, questionable authorship) and the disclosure/retention requirements that can lead to retraction or other editorial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an LLM should be properly documented in the Methods section (and if a Methods section is not available, in a suitable alternative part) of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Neurosurgical Review author submission guidelines: the use of an LLM (or other AI-tool) for “AI assisted copy editing” purposes does not need to be declared. In all cases, there must be human accountability for the final version of the text and agreement from the authors that the edits reflect their original work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human accountability for final text
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be human accountability for the final version of the text and agreement from the authors that the edits reflect their original work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if AI tools are used, authors must take responsibility for and approve the final manuscript; failure to have human accountability or agreement that edits reflect original work can constitute a breach of editorial policy (and lead to retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction grounds for serious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions are meant for serious misconduct — fabricated data, plagiarism, or harmful misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal/publisher practice treats fabrication, plagiarism, and misinformation as canonical grounds for retraction; there is debate whether undisclosed AI assistance alone should trigger retraction if it does not cause those harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal clustering of submissions as a red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that arrive over a short space of time can indicate problematic mass-generated content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices cited investigations finding 'a number of articles ... submitted over a short space of time' as evidence of coordinated or automated generation; journals may treat rapid bursts of similar submissions as suspicious and investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual indicators of LLM generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong indications that the text was generated by a large language model (LLM) without proper disclosure constitutes a breach of editorial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers investigate for wording, phrasing, or other stylistic/structural signs that suggest LLM output; such indications plus lack of disclosure have led to retractions in the cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation stacking / citation manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Including unnecessary citations to bolster metrics, including self-citation, is considered improper citation stacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an article whose original submission cited zero papers by an author but the revised version added ten of that author's papers—this pattern prompted an Elsevier audit and retraction. Audits and investigations of unusual citation growth can lead to retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant increase in author-self citations between versions
rubrics_metrics.description: A large increase in citations to papers by an author between the original submission and the revised version is a red flag for citation manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may request explanations for added citations; inability to explain or unjustified additions (especially added without co-author approval) can cause loss of confidence and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclear or difficult-to-parse passages as a quality/integrity concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases that make some passages in the article difficult to parse can undermine confidence in the article's findings or integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors cannot explain odd phrasing or unclear passages (which may be indicative of automated text insertion or poor revision), editors may judge the article unreliable and retract it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper authorship practices and co-author approval
rubrics_metrics.description: All authors should be aware of and approve substantive changes (including added citations) made during revision; questionable authorship practices are flagged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a co-author reported being unaware that additional citations were added by the corresponding author during revision; such lack of co-author approval or involvement can be considered questionable authorship practice and trigger investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial operational responses to suspected misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may pause acceptance of certain article types (e.g., letters, commentaries) when overwhelmed by suspected AI-generated submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a precautionary or investigative response, a journal may halt submissions in affected categories until policies/processes are clarified and investigations are completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher investigation -> breach of editorial policy -> retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings from a publisher's investigation that articles were generated by LLMs without proper disclosure can be deemed a breach of the Journal’s editorial policy and lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices explicitly cite publisher investigations and policy breaches; investigations may be ongoing and further editorial action may follow based on emerging evidence.
